lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Three pots are wet, then dry, then dry. Start watered at 0 and use the same dry-soil decision. What is watered after each pot, and what is the final count?

FEEDBACK
Wet, dry, then dry makes watered stay 0, become 1, then finish at 2, because only the two dry pots receive a cup. Pot 1 is wet, so watered stays 0. Pot 2 is dry, so watered becomes 1. Pot 3 is dry, so watered becomes 2. All 3 pots are visited. Pouring on the wet pot would ignore the decision and make the count 3, which this algorithm does not do.

WATCH FOR
A common mistake is to water every plant, or to skip the count, so the dry-soil decision never changes the result. The decision chooses the cup. The count records only the plants that received water.

teaching.feedback: Wet, dry, then dry makes watered stay 0, become 1, then finish at 2, because only the two dry pots receive a cup. Pot 1 is wet, so watered stays 0. Pot 2 is dry, so watered becomes 1. Pot 3 is dry, so watered becomes 2. All 3 pots are visited. Pouring on the wet pot would ignore the decision and make the count 3, which this algorithm does not do.
teaching.fix: Correct the claim, criteria use or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
teaching.guided_attempt: Describe why the warned-against claim fails, then write a corrected claim with evidence.
teaching.misconception: Changing the wording without repairing the evidence does not fix the error. A common mistake is to water every plant, or to skip the count, so the dry-soil decision never changes the result. The decision chooses the cup. The count records only the plants that received water.
teaching.model: A common mistake is to water every plant, or to skip the count, so the dry-soil decision never changes the result. The decision chooses the cup. The count records only the plants that received water. Here is a more productive model: Dry, wet, then dry plants make the watered count go 0, 1, 1 and finish at 2, with all three plants visited. Start watered at 0. Plant A is dry, so pour one cup and watered becomes 1. Plant B is wet, so pour nothing and watered stays 1. Plant C is dry, so pour one cup and watered becomes 2. The visit count is 3. The watered count ends at 2. Wet soil is a real decision, not a skipped plant.

If the soil is dry, pour one cup and add 1 to watered. If the soil is not dry, add 0. Work on paper only. Now choose a different example to show you can transfer the idea.
